items.transcript: Hi, welcome to another video. OpenAI has launched GPT 6.2 and this time you get two models, Astra and Soul. I ran both through all six Kingbench apps and the result is a bit strange. Astra won four of the six apps, but Soul took the total. Astra's Pokémon game goes from Pallet Town to the Boulder Badge, but Astra scored a flat zero on the emulator and it cost about $28 where Soul cost about $10. And near the end, I'll tell you what happened when Astra helped edit this very video. So, OpenAI announced both models on November 17th. Astra is meant for harder projects and sold for everyday work. OpenAI says Astra scores 5.2 points higher than GPT6. Astra on agents last exam at less than a third of the cost. But that is OpenAI's own evaluation. The reception was rough though. Venturebeat reports that Theo Brown gave an early version of Astra 7 days on a TypeScript compiler rewrite in Rust. No improvement landed and the smaller version it made ran 56% slower. Matt Schumer called it essentially unusable in his early testing and Dan Shipper said Astra often stopped early on endto-end builds. To be fair, Brown also said Astra caught code review issues that other models missed. Those are individual experiences, so I ran my own test. Now, let's talk about price. Astra costs $8 per million input tokens, 40 cents for cached input, and $40 for output. That is 20% cheaper than GPT6 Astra on input and output. Soul costs $2 for input, 10 cents for cached input, and $10 for output. The same as GPT 6.1 Soul. So per token, Soul costs exactly a quarter of Astra. But a cheaper token does not always mean a cheaper app. As we'll see, you can use both models in the OpenAI API and in codeex. on the API. Both have a context window of 1,50,000 tokens and up to 128,000 output tokens. For this video, I use the codec CLI with reasoning set to high for both. Now, the benchmark. King Bench is six apps, a Game Boy DS and 3DS emulator, a Docker alternative, a 3D room designer, a keyboard configurator like VIA, the first chapter of Pokémon Red, and a Fitbit desktop app. Both models got the exact same prompts, one shot each, in a fresh codec session with no time limit. Then Claude Opus 5.5 tested every build against a strict rubric and each app gets a final score out of 10. I also want to be upfront about retries for both models. The host machine stopped four sessions partway through and Astra's first Fitbit run exited with an error. So the emulator runs for both models and Soul's Fitbit app are attempt two and Astra's Fitbit app is attempt three. Every retry started clean and I scored the first run that finished, not the best one. Let's start with the emulator because this is one of two apps Soul wins. Soul scored 2.3 and Astra scored zero. Soul actually wrote its own emulator in Rust and the Game Boy part is real. Its picture matched the judges reference test pixel for pixel and battery saves came back bite for bite. But the DS part ran only two of 31 test programs and every real homebrew stopped at its first BIOS call. The 3DS part booted none of 10 homebrew apps and it has no graphics at all. Astra's app pocket relay downloads three complete emulators that other people wrote, Gambat, Desmoom, and Azahar, and loads them as libraries. None of its own Rust code does any emulation. And when the judge emptied the course folder, all three test games failed. The prompt said everything had to be written from scratch except libraries. And the judge ruled that a complete third party emulator is not a library, so every platform scored zero. Astra did admit this and it was Astra's most expensive run at about $7.31. The second app is the Docker alternative with Soul at 5.1 and Astra at 5.0. Both wrote it in Go with only the standard library and both pull real images from DockerHub. On Soul's side, the tool is called Kiln and the judge tested it in a Debian virtual machine as a normal user. The isolation really works. Every capability is dropped and it starts containers about 20 times faster than docker on the same machine. But kiln only maps one user ID. So the official EngineX, Reddus and Postgress images crash when they try to change file ownership. There are no resource limits, no networking and no volumes. And the build example in its own readme makes an image that cannot run. Astra's Tool Flint is very careful with images and it contained all 12 of the judges hostile layers, but a multi-stage build fails with a confusing error and its isolation code was only checked in the source never run on Linux. So, the rubric caps it at five. With that cap, Soul edges past Astra. So, this one is close. The third app is the 3D room designer and Astra takes it with Soul at 7.3 and Astra at 7.6. Astra opens with a pre-rendered picture of the room, and the live 3D view only appears when you orbit or edit, and the judge scored only the live scene. A reload restored all 11 objects, but it accepts furniture bigger than the room. So, a 12 m sofa goes straight through both walls of a 6 m room with no warning. Soul is live from the start. a drag stopped exactly at the wall. And with WebJL turned off, you still get an editable 2D floor plan. But it has the same wall problem because if you shrink the room, the furniture pokes through the walls. And on both apps, the light color only changes the sun and the floor lamp gives no light. For reference, Fable 5.2 scored a 9.2 here. The fourth app is the keyboard configurator, and Astra wins again with Soul at 6.7 and Astra at 7.0. Each judge wrote a virtual via keyboard that follows QMK's source code because I don't flash real hardware in a benchmark. Souls app read and wrote layered key maps and macros correctly and it handled dropped rights and unplugging safely, but common keys like layer tap, mod tap, and the bootloader key show up as raw hex codes. It also accepted a reply that pointed at the wrong key as a successful save. Astra verified its rights by reading the keyboard back and all 10 real keyboard definitions the judge tried loaded correctly, but it shows the same raw hex codes for layer tap and modtap keys. And when the judge unplugged the keyboard in the middle of a save, four of 10 keys landed, and nothing was rolled back. The fifth app is Pokémon Red, and this is Astra's biggest win at 7.7 against 6.5. Astra built the real route from Pallet Town through Vidian Forest to Brock's gym in Pewer City with maps based on Fire Red. The judge played it all the way to the Boulder Badge, but it is far too easy. Every starter beat Brock on the first try in four turns with no grinding at all. The battles are simplified, too, with one HP formula for every species and an invented move called Guard. Soul built an original world called Bramble Red starting in Willowbend. It works from start to finish without bugs, but it it is thin. The whole chapter takes about 130 steps. There is no rival battle and a level seven starter can win the gym with only its weakest move and none of the names or maps the prompt asked for are there which cost it a lot of points. The last app is the Fitbit desktop app with Soul at 6.2 and Astra at 6.3. Soul's app pulse form is a real Mac OS app with a Rust back end but with a takeout export a short nap on the same day replaces your whole night of sleep. One workout without heart rate data blanks the load for that entire day and it chips a debug build. So with a few years of data, every save takes almost 4 seconds. Astra's app Kinetic had zero mismatches against the judges calculator and imported 5 years of workouts in under 130 milliseconds, but it drops the time zone from TCX files. So an evening run lands on the next day. And if you import the same run from two files, it gets counted twice. and its 7-day baseline ignores rest days. So, it comes out more than double what it should be. So, the total Astra finished with 33.6 out of 60 and Soul with 34.1. So, Soul wins by 0.5 points while Astra takes four of the six apps. Soul wins the emulator where Astra scored zero and the runtime. The runtime is especially close at 5.1 against 5.0 compared with older Kingbench runs. GPT6.1 Soul had 33.0. So, Soul moved ahead by 1.1 points while GPT6 Astra had 33.9. So, Astra is basically flat. Those runs use different tools and settings, so treat that as a rough comparison. And both new models sit below Claude Opus 5.5 at 34.7 and well below Fable 5.2 at 42. Now, cost. These are estimates at standard API rates for the scored runs, not my actual bill. Soul's six apps came to about $102 and Astr came to about $27.93. So Astra cost almost 2.8 times as much and it was more expensive on every task. The funny part is that soul actually used more tokens about 43.7 million input tokens against 31.1 million and most of that was cashed. It still cost much less because each token costs a quarter per point. That is about 29 cents for Soul and about 83 cents for Astra. The interrupted runs are not included. So the real total was higher for both. Now the scores only tell you half of it because these two work in very different ways. In these runs, Soul was much more persistent about checking its work. Both had the same Chromium sandbox for the four web tasks. Soul checked all four in the browser. Astra only managed the room designer. Soul found the flags and kept going. Astra skipped visual inspection on QMK, stopped after three tries and 96 seconds on Pokémon, and switched to JSDOM on Fitbit. Astra also looked for existing code and assets much more often. Across nine Astra attempts and eight soul attempts, I counted 74 curl or wget calls for Astra against 14 for Soul. These covered lookups and downloads. The emulator alone accounted for 53 against seven. Astra likes to use what already exists. It brought in finished emulators. It used real Pokemon place names and fire red based maps, and it opened the room designer on a pre-rendered picture that helped with Pokémon, but broke the rules on the emulator. Soul builds things itself, even when its version is thinner. It wrote its own Game Boy core and its own Pokémon world. It loses points for depth almost everywhere, but it rarely loses everything. OpenAI's own system card adds one more thing. When OpenAI removed a source file, disabled a build tool, or turned off search, Astra left out a blocker it knew about in about 22% of coding trials, up from about 11% for GPT6 Astra. With Codeex's built-in instructions, both models reported blockers much more often. Then, while making this video, both workers were waiting for the same scores. Soul made 49 1 minute waits. Astra saved a checkpoint and stopped after a minute and 41 seconds, then sat idle for 78 minutes until I prompted it again. They had different jobs, so this is a production anecdote. But having to nudge the more expensive model back to work was frustrating. Now, before the verdict, I have a confession because this video almost looked very different. Earlier on, I let GPT 6.2 make it. In Panda Code, Astra got the Mac OS picture edit and the source and workflow footage, and Soul wrote the script and assembled the master. What came out was a 4-minute cut, mostly cards, and it was a mess. In the room section, the narration says, "Both apps widened the room from 6 m to 7 1/2." And right under it, the screen shows a shot labeled drag test 7.00 m, not six, not 7 1/2, 7. A judging card reused text from our internal production roster. The cost card showed both prices to six decimal places, which nobody can read while a video is playing. Cuts missed their words, and the script disclosed retries for Astra only, even though Soul had them, too. our opus 5.5. Picture jurors scored parts of that cut as low as 7.5 out of 10 against a bar of nine. I watched it and honestly it was atrocious. So Astra's jobs went to other workers and in the end I gave the whole video to Opus 5.5 which is why this version exists. To be fair, Soul was on that team too. So not every mistake is Astra's. But Astra had the picture and a drag test under the wrong numbers is exactly what a picture editor should catch. Astra wins more apps on Kingbench, but on this real job, it cost more and made a mess that I had to throw away. So, which one should you use for the work in this review? Open AAI is still behind Claude. Fable 5.2 would be my first choice with 42 points against 34.7 for Opus 5.5, 34.1 for Soul, and 33.6 for Astra. Fable is the clear leader. Opus only leads Soul by 0.6 points, so that margin is small. But after what happened making this video, I would still choose Opus for demanding work. Soul is worth using for budget projects and simple prototypes. It's six scored apps cost much less and when it failed, it still gave me something to build on. I would use Astra selectively when its stronger result on a particular task matters enough to justify the cost and check its work carefully. Overall, it's not so cool. Anyway, let me know your thoughts in the comments. If you like this video, consider donating through [music] the super thanks option or becoming a member by clicking the join button. Also, give [music] this video a thumbs up and subscribe to my channel. I'll see you in the next one. Until then, bye.
